Long-term goals to keep in mind\n\nFrom `docs/requirements/lab5-notes-final-presentation.png` (the final presentation):\n\n- a PowerPoint presentation that is **fun and creative**, even **a bit funny**\n- an **interesting interface**\n- **not only exactly what is asked**: a good project that **stands out**\n- a **good research part**\n- all criteria met; aiming for a **10**, by being **very creative**\n\nWhat this means for Deliverable 2:\n- Build the core cleanly; everything later (interface, dataset, parser) stands on it.\n- Keep visual output from day one (images and GIFs of runs). It is cheap, and it becomes material for the final presentation.\n- Start the research part early: the engine can already measure cycle statistics for all 256 elementary rules (stretch goal, section 16), which previews the Deliverable 3 experiment.\n- Make the Deliverable 2 demo memorable: live, short, with a couple of moments people remember (section 15).\n\n---\n\n## 3. Design overview\n\nTwo kinds of input files, kept separate:\n\n- **Automaton spec** (`automata/*.json`): *what the automaton is*. States, neighbourhood, edges, rules, rule parameters.\n- **Experiment file** (`experiments/*.json`): *what we do with it*. Grid size, initial world, number of steps, seed, storage options, the questions to answer.\n\nOne automaton can be used in many experiments, and an experiment can be rerun exactly.\n\n```\nautomaton spec ─┐\n                ├─► validator ─► engine ─► fingerprints ─► answers to the 5 questions\nexperiment file ┘                  │\n                                   └─► run folder: checkpoints, stored generations, answers, images\n                                          ▲\n                              cellab resume ┘  (continues from the last checkpoint)\n```\n\n---\n\n## 4. The automaton spec format\n\nJSON, because the Deliverable 4 parser will produce JSON and it needs no extra library.\n\n### Structure\n| Field | Meaning | Values |\n|---|---|---|\n| `name` | Display name | text |\n| `dimensions` | 1 or 2 | `1`, `2` |\n| `states` | Possible cell values | a list of names (`[\"EMPTY\",\"TREE\",\"FIRE\"]`), or `{\"type\": \"integer\", \"min\": 0}`, or `{\"type\": \"real\"}` |\n| `neighbourhood` | Which cells a cell sees | `\"elementary\"` (left, self, right), `\"von_neumann\"` (4), `\"moore\"` (8), or a list of offsets |\n| `edges` | What lies beyond the grid | `{\"type\": \"wrap\"}` or `{\"type\": \"fixed\", \"value\": ...}` |\n| `parameters` | Named numbers used in rules | e.g. `{\"p\": 0.01}` |\n| `rules` | Ordered list; the first matching rule wins | `{\"when\": <condition>, \"then\": <new value>}` or a pattern `table` |\n| `otherwise` | Value when no rule matches | default `\"self\"` (unchanged) |\n\n### The rule language\nRules are small expressions, evaluated for the whole grid at once with NumPy:\n\n- **Cell values:** `self`; in 1D also `left` and `right`.\n- **Neighbour aggregates:** `count(<condition on nb>)`, `sum(nb)`, `mean(nb)`, `min(nb)`, `max(nb)`. Inside them, `nb` stands for each neighbour in turn. `count(FIRE)` is short for `count(nb == FIRE)`.\n- **Names:** declared state names and `parameters`.\n- **Operators:** `+ - * / // % **`, comparisons, `and or not`, `x if c else y`.\n- **Functions:** `random()` (seeded, section 8), `abs`, `round`, `floor`.\n\n**How it's implemented:** Python's own `ast` module parses each expression. Only a whitelist of node types is allowed, so the input can't run arbitrary code. The expression is then compiled into NumPy operations, so we don't write a parser from scratch.\n\n**Rule semantics:** start from `otherwise`, then apply the rules from last to first with `np.where`, so earlier rules take precedence.\n\n### Examples\n**Forest fire** (deterministic, from the brief):\n```json\n{\n  \"name\": \"Forest fire\",\n  \"dimensions\": 2,\n  \"states\": [\"EMPTY\", \"TREE\", \"FIRE\"],\n  \"neighbourhood\": \"von_neumann\",\n  \"edges\": {\"type\": \"fixed\", \"value\": \"EMPTY\"},\n  \"rules\": [\n    {\"when\": \"self == FIRE\", \"then\": \"EMPTY\"},\n    {\"when\": \"self == TREE and count(FIRE) >= 1\", \"then\": \"FIRE\"}\n  ],\n  \"otherwise\": \"self\"\n}\n```\n\n**Forest fire with regrowth and lightning** (random; the same file plus parameters):\n```json\n\"parameters\": {\"p\": 0.01, \"f\": 0.0001},\n\"rules\": [\n  {\"when\": \"self == FIRE\", \"then\": \"EMPTY\"},\n  {\"when\": \"self == TREE and (count(FIRE) >= 1 or random() < f)\", \"then\": \"FIRE\"},\n  {\"when\": \"self == EMPTY and random() < p\", \"then\": \"TREE\"}\n]\n```\n\n**Rule 30** (the brief's truth table, written as a pattern table of left, self, right):\n```json\n{\n  \"name\": \"Rule 30\",\n  \"dimensions\": 1,\n  \"states\": [0, 1],\n  \"neighbourhood\": \"elementary\",\n  \"edges\": {\"type\": \"fixed\", \"value\": 0},\n  \"rules\": [{\"table\": {\"111\": 0, \"110\": 0, \"101\": 0, \"100\": 1,\n                       \"011\": 1, \"010\": 1, \"001\": 1, \"000\": 0}}]\n}\n```\n\n**Brian's Brain:**\n```json\n\"states\": [\"OFF\", \"FIRING\", \"DYING\"],\n\"neighbourhood\": \"moore\",\n\"rules\": [\n  {\"when\": \"self == FIRING\", \"then\": \"DYING\"},\n  {\"when\": \"self == DYING\", \"then\": \"OFF\"},\n  {\"when\": \"self == OFF and count(FIRING) == 2\", \"then\": \"FIRING\"}\n]\n```\n\n**Sandpile** (numeric; all unstable cells topple at once, grains falling off the edge are lost):\n```json\n\"states\": {\"type\": \"integer\", \"min\": 0},\n\"neighbourhood\": \"von_neumann\",\n\"edges\": {\"type\": \"fixed\", \"value\": 0},\n\"rules\": [{\"then\": \"self - 4 * (self >= 4) + count(nb >= 4)\"}]\n```\n\n**Cyclic, 4 states:**\n```json\n\"states\": {\"type\": \"integer\", \"min\": 0, \"max\": 3},\n\"neighbourhood\": \"moore\",\n\"rules\": [{\"when\": \"count(nb == (self + 1) % 4) >= 2\", \"then\": \"(self + 1) % 4\"}]\n```\n\nThe same language covers voter, crystal growth, epidemic (infection timers as states I1, I2, I3), diffusion, traffic (Rule 184) and Game of Life, all without new code.\n\n---\n\n## 5. The experiment file (parameters and the 5 questions)\n\n```json\n{\n  \"name\": \"Forest fire, grid from the brief\",\n  \"automaton\": \"../automata/forest_fire.json\",\n  \"grid\": {\"width\": 5, \"height\": 4},\n  \"initial\": {\n    \"type\": \"text\",\n    \"rows\": [\"TTTT.\", \"TT.TT\", \".TFTT\", \"TTTTT\"],\n    \"legend\": {\"T\": \"TREE\", \"F\": \"FIRE\", \".\": \"EMPTY\"}\n  },\n  \"steps\": 20,\n  \"max_steps\": 100000,\n  \"seed\": 42,\n  \"store_generations\": true,\n  \"checkpoint_every\": 10,\n  \"questions\": [\n    {\"ask\": \"state_after\", \"n\": 2},\n    {\"ask\": \"stable_when\"},\n    {\"ask\": \"occurs\", \"configuration\": {\"rows\": [\"T....\", \".....\", \".....\", \".....\"]}},\n    {\"ask\": \"count_after\", \"state\": \"TREE\", \"n\": 3},\n    {\"ask\": \"cycle\"}\n  ]\n}\n```\n\n**Initial world types:**\n- `text`: rows with a legend\n- `random`: with `weights` per state, e.g. `{\"TREE\": 0.7, \"EMPTY\": 0.3}`\n- `single`: one cell of a given state in the centre\n- `file`: a saved grid or generation\n\n`max_steps` is the budget for questions that may need a long run. The seed is always recorded: if the file has none, we generate one and write it into the run folder.\n\n---\n\n## 6. The engine\n\n- **Grid storage:**\n  - named states are stored as `uint8` indices\n  - integer states as `int32`\n  - real states as `float64`, with an optional rounding setting (the brief's diffusion example rounds to whole numbers)\n- **Neighbourhoods** are lists of offsets. Edges are handled by padding the grid (`np.pad` with `wrap` or a constant). Each neighbour is then a shifted view of the padded array, so the code is the same for 1D and 2D and for any neighbourhood.\n- **One step:** evaluate every rule's condition and value on the old grid, then build the new grid. All cells update at the same time, as the brief describes.\n- **Update modes:** Deliverable 2 implements the synchronous mode, which covers 10–11 of the 15 examples. Movement (traffic with speeds, falling sand) and agents (Langton's ant, predator–prey, Schelling, ecosystem) come later. Their file format is designed now, so the presentation can show it extends (section 16).\n- **Performance:** fully vectorised, so a 200 × 200 grid for 1,000 steps takes seconds.\n\n---\n\n## 7. Fingerprints (hashes) and the five questions\n\n- **Fingerprint of a state:** `blake2b` (16 bytes) of the grid bytes plus its shape and data type. That's fast, and the chance of two different states colliding is negligible. On a match we still compare the stored grids when they are available.\n- **Fingerprint table:** maps each fingerprint to the step where it first appeared, kept in memory and saved in every checkpoint. At 16 bytes per step, a million steps take 16 MB.\n- **The five questions:**\n  1. **State after N:** simulate to N. If a cycle is already known and N is huge, jump ahead: state(N) = state(μ + (N − μ) mod λ).\n  2. **When is it stable:** the first step t where state(t+1) = state(t). Possible answers: \"never: it enters a cycle of length λ\", or \"not decided within `max_steps`\".\n  3. **Does C occur:** fingerprint C and look it up. If the cycle closed without C appearing, the answer is a certain **never**.\n  4. **Count of type X after N:** state after N, then count.\n  5. **Does it enter a cycle:** the first repeated fingerprint gives the run-up length μ and the cycle length λ.\n- **For random rules:** a repeated grid is not a true cycle, because the random numbers continue. Answers for random automata say so explicitly. This is a good detail to mention, and it links to the statistics planned for later.\n- **Fallback:** if a cycle is too long to keep in memory, use Brent's algorithm (stretch).\n\n---\n\n## 8. Fixed randomness (same seed, same result)\n\n- **One generator per run:** `numpy.random.Generator(PCG64(seed))`. Nothing uses Python's `random` or NumPy's global functions; a test checks this.\n- **Fixed order of random draws:** the random initial world is drawn first. Then, each step, one full-grid array per `random()` call site, in rule order. Draws depend only on the step, never on timing or dictionary order.\n- **The generator's internal state** (a small dictionary) is saved in every checkpoint, so a resumed run continues the same random sequence.\n- **Shown three ways:**\n  - **Test:** two runs with the same seed produce identical fingerprint sequences.\n  - **Test:** different seeds produce different runs.\n  - **Live:** two terminals side by side print the same fingerprints.\n\n---\n\n## 9. Saving, reloading and resuming\n\nEach run gets its own folder, so it's self-contained and reproducible:\n```\nruns/forest_fire_brief/2026-11-03_14-05-12/\n  automaton.json        copy of the spec used\n  experiment.json       copy of the experiment, including the seed actually used\n  checkpoint.npz        current grid, step, generator state, fingerprint list, spec digest\n  generations.npz       stored generations (compressed; 2-state grids bit-packed), if enabled\n  answers.json          answers to the questions\n  run.log\n```\n- **Checkpoints:**\n  - written every `checkpoint_every` steps and when the run is interrupted with Ctrl+C\n  - written atomically (to a temporary file, then renamed), so a crash never leaves a broken checkpoint\n- **Resume:** `cellab resume <run folder> [--steps K]` continues from the last checkpoint. It refuses if the automaton spec changed since (it compares the spec digest).\n- **Key guarantee, tested:** run 100 steps in one go, versus run 40, stop, reload, run 60 more. The fingerprints and answers must be identical.\n- **Extra:** start a new experiment from any stored generation (`\"initial\": {\"type\": \"file\", ...}`), e.g. \"what happens from step 40 with a different seed\".\n\n---\n\n## 10. Validation\n\nChecked when a file is loaded, before anything runs. This is the constraint satisfaction topic from Lab 5.\n\n- **Structure:** required fields, correct types, allowed values (`pydantic` models).\n- **Meaning:**\n  - every name used in a rule is a declared state, a parameter or a built-in\n  - rule values fall within the declared states or range\n  - the edge value is a valid state\n  - the initial world uses only valid states and fits the grid\n  - question parameters make sense (X is a state, C matches the grid size, N ≥ 0)\n- **Messages name the file, the field and the problem.** For example: `forest_fire.json, rules[1].when: unknown name 'FLAME' (states are EMPTY, TREE, FIRE)`.\n- **A folder of deliberately broken files** in the tests, each with the error it must produce.\n\n---\n\n## 11. Which automata\n\n| Priority | Automata | Why |\n|---|---|---|\n| **Required (3)** | Rule 30, forest fire (deterministic + random), Brian's Brain | 1D and 2D, named states, randomness, and the brief's \"harder automaton\" |\n| **Planned** | Sandpile, cyclic, voter, crystal growth, epidemic, diffusion, traffic (Rule 184) | Each is only a new file, which proves the engine is general |\n| **Bonus** | Game of Life | Not in the brief's list; shows the system handles automata it wasn't built around |\n| **Stretch** | Langton's ant | Needs the agent mode; at least show its file format |\n\nEach automaton gets a spec file and an experiment file. Where the brief gives a starting grid, the experiment uses it.\n\n---\n\n## 12. Code layout and interfaces\n\n```\ncellab/\n  spec.py           load + validate automaton specs\n  experiment.py     load + validate experiment files\n  expressions.py    safe rule expressions → NumPy\n  neighbourhood.py  offsets, edges, padding\n  engine.py         one step, the run loop\n  randomness.py     seeded generator, saving/restoring its state\n  fingerprints.py   state hashing, fingerprint table, cycle detection\n  questions.py      the five questions\n  storage.py        run folders, checkpoints, resume\n  render.py         text, PNG and GIF output\n  cli.py            `cellab check | run | resume | render`\nautomata/           spec files\nexperiments/        experiment files\ntests/\n```\n\nAgree on these on day 1, so both of us can work in parallel:\n```python\nspec = load_spec(path)                      # -> Spec (validated)\nexp = load_experiment(path)                 # -> Experiment (validated, spec loaded)\nstate = initial_state(spec, exp, rng)       # -> np.ndarray\nnew = step(spec, state, rng)                # -> np.ndarray, pure apart from rng draws\nfp = fingerprint(state)                     # -> bytes (16)\nresult = run(spec, exp, run_dir)            # -> RunResult (fingerprints, answers, final state)\nresult = resume(run_dir, extra_steps)       # -> RunResult\n```\n\n**Command line:**\n- `cellab check automata/forest_fire.json`: validate only.\n- `cellab run experiments/forest_fire_brief.json`: run, answer, save.\n- `cellab resume runs/.../<run>`: continue after a stop.\n- `cellab render runs/.../<run> --gif`: images and an animation of the run.\n\n**Dependencies:** numpy, pydantic, pillow, pytest, in a `requirements.txt` with pinned versions. I've written the full plan to [docs/deliverables/D2-modeling/PLAN.md](docs/deliverables/D2-modeling/PLAN.md), and saved both photos of your notes in `docs/requirements/`. Here's the core of it.

## What your Lab 5 notes ask for

| Note | What it means |
|---|---|
| Rules read from files; no automaton-specific code; input files | Each automaton is a file, run by one general engine |
| Save the state; reload and continue from where it stopped | Checkpoints plus a `resume` command |
| State the parameters, including the 5 questions | An experiment file holding the grid, initial world, steps, seed and the 5 questions |
| 2–3 of the 15 automata ("I'd do more") | 3 required, 10+ planned |
| Hashes over states → maximum score | A fingerprint of every state, used to answer the questions |
| Fixed randomness: same seed twice, same result → maximum score | One seeded random generator, saved with every checkpoint |

## The main design choices
1. **Two input files.** The *automaton spec* says what the automaton is. The *experiment file* says what to do with it: grid, start, steps, seed, which questions to ask.
2. **Rules are small expressions.** For example: `{"when": "self == TREE and count(FIRE) >= 1", "then": "FIRE"}`. One engine evaluates them for the whole grid at once.
   - The same rule language covers Rule 30, forest fire, Brian's Brain, the sandpile, cyclic, voter, crystal growth, epidemic, diffusion, traffic, and even Game of Life.
   - So each new automaton is just a new file. That's the strongest evidence for "nothing automaton-specific in the code".
3. **A fingerprint (hash) of every state.** The fingerprints give stable states, cycles and "does C ever occur" (including a certain "never"). They also let the engine jump ahead to very large N.
4. **One seeded random generator, saved in every checkpoint.** A run that is stopped and resumed gives exactly the same result as one that never stopped.
5. **A test that fails if any automaton name** (`TREE`, `FIRE`, …) **appears in the engine code.** It proves generality, and it'll make a good slide.

## The week
- **Day 1, together:** agree on the file formats and the function interfaces, so you can then work in parallel.
- **Days 2–5, split in two:**
  - files, validation and saving/resuming
  - engine, fingerprints and the 5 questions
- **Day 4:** first integration. The three required automata run end to end.
- **Day 6:** add 7–8 more automata (files only) and their tests.
- **Day 7:** slides, demo rehearsal, and push.

**Tests:** several of them check results we already computed: your Rule 58 example, the Rule 30 cycle lengths, the forest fire answers, and the brief's sandpile grid.

## Thinking ahead to the final presentation
Your second set of notes asks for fun, creativity, an interesting interface, and a strong research part. The plan already builds toward these:

## Assistant (2026-10-29T22:04:52.093Z)

Practically, Deliverable 2 is a small Python package (about 800 lines plus tests), a set of input files, and a short demo. Below is the architecture, then the build steps in the order they depend on each other. Each step says what to write and how to know it's done.

## The architecture in one picture

```
 automata/forest_fire.json      experiments/forest_fire_brief.json
            │                                │
            ▼                                ▼
   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ 1. INPUT      spec.py, experiment.py            │  read JSON → validated objects
   │               (pydantic models + checks)        │  (errors stop here, with clear messages)
   ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
   │ 2. RULES      expressions.py                    │  "self == TREE and count(FIRE) >= 1"
   │               (Python ast → NumPy evaluation)   │  → whole-grid boolean array
   ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
   │ 3. CORE       neighbourhood.py, engine.py       │  step(grid) → new grid
   │               randomness.py                     │  (pure, apart from seeded random draws)
   ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
   │ 4. RUN        fingerprints.py, questions.py,    │  loop: step → fingerprint → answer
   │               storage.py                        │  → checkpoint → (Ctrl+C) → resume
   ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
   │ 5. OUTSIDE    cli.py, render.py                 │  `cellab run / resume / check / render`
   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                         │
                         ▼
   runs/<experiment>/<time>/  checkpoint.npz, generations.npz, answers.json, run.gif
```

**The rule:** each layer only uses the layers above it. The engine never knows about files, and the input layer never knows about NumPy grids. This separation is what lets you build the two halves in parallel.

**The four objects that pass between layers:**
- `Spec`: the validated automaton (states, neighbour offsets, compiled rules).
- `Experiment`: the validated parameters (grid size, initial world, steps, seed, questions).
- `grid`: a plain NumPy array (`uint8` for named states, `int32` or `float64` for numbers).
- `RunState`: step number, grid, random generator, fingerprint list, answers so far. This is exactly what a checkpoint saves.

---

## Step 0: project setup (day 1, about 1 hour)

```bash
python -m venv .venv
```
- Activate it: `.venv\Scripts\activate` on Windows, `source .venv/bin/activate` on Linux.
- Install the dependencies: `pip install numpy pydantic pillow pytest`, then `pip freeze > requirements.txt`.
- Add a `pyproject.toml` with the entry point `cellab = "cellab.cli:main"`. Then `pip install -e .` makes `cellab ...` work as a command.
- Add `.venv/` and `runs/` to `.gitignore`.
- Create empty modules under `cellab/` and a `tests/` folder.

**Done when:** `pytest` runs (0 tests) on both laptops.

## Step 1: write the input files first (day 1)

Before writing any code, write the three required automata and their experiment files by hand, in the format from the plan (section 4):
- `automata/rule30.json`, `forest_fire.json`, `brians_brain.json`
- `experiments/` with the starting grids from the brief

These files are the specification of the code: every feature the engine needs appears in them. If a file is awkward to write, change the format now, while it costs nothing.

**Done when:** you both agree on the three files and freeze the format.

## Step 2: loading and validation (`spec.py`, `experiment.py`)

**Structure:** pydantic models do the type checks for free.
```python
class Edges(BaseModel):
    type: Literal["wrap", "fixed"]
    value: str | int | float | None = None

class Rule(BaseModel):
    when: str = "True"                    # no condition = always
    then: str | int | float | None = None
    table: dict[str, str | int] | None = None

class SpecFile(BaseModel):
    name: str
    dimensions: Literal[1, 2]
    states: list[str | int] | NumericStates
    neighbourhood: Literal["elementary", "von_neumann", "moore"] | list[list[int]]
    edges: Edges
    parameters: dict[str, float] = {}
    rules: list[Rule]
    otherwise: str = "self"
```

**Meaning checks**, done after the structure checks:
- state names become indices (`EMPTY=0, TREE=1, FIRE=2`)
- neighbourhood names become offset lists
- every expression is compiled (step 3), which catches unknown names
- the edge value must be a valid state
- each table key must be as long as the neighbourhood

**The experiment loader:**
- resolves the `automaton` path relative to the experiment file
- checks the initial world fits the grid and uses valid states
- checks the question parameters (X is a state, C matches the grid size, N ≥ 0)

**Done when:** `load_experiment("experiments/forest_fire_brief.json")` returns objects, and a deliberately broken file gives a message like `forest_fire.json, rules[1].when: unknown name 'FLAME'`.

## Step 3: the rule language (`expressions.py`)

This is the heart of "nothing automaton-specific in the code". Python's `ast` module parses the expression, a whitelist rejects anything dangerous, and a small recursive function evaluates it with NumPy arrays:

```python
ALLOWED = (ast.Expression, ast.BoolOp, ast.BinOp, ast.UnaryOp, ast.Compare, ast.IfExp,
           ast.Call, ast.Name, ast.Constant, ast.Load, ast.And, ast.Or, ast.Not, ast.USub,
           ast.Add, ast.Sub, ast.Mult, ast.Div, ast.FloorDiv, ast.Mod, ast.Pow,
           ast.Eq, ast.NotEq, ast.Lt, ast.LtE, ast.Gt, ast.GtE)

def compile_expr(text, known_names):
    tree = ast.parse(text, mode="eval")
    for node in ast.walk(tree):
        if not isinstance(node, ALLOWED):
            raise SpecError(f"'{text}': {type(node).__name__} is not allowed")
        if isinstance(node, ast.Name) and node.id not in known_names:
            raise SpecError(f"'{text}': unknown name '{node.id}'")
    return tree.body

def evaluate(node, ctx):
    match node:
        case ast.Constant(): return node.value
        case ast.Name():     return ctx.lookup(node.id)   # self, nb, left, right, state, parameter
        case ast.BinOp():    return BINARY[type(node.op)](evaluate(node.left, ctx), evaluate(node.right, ctx))
        case ast.BoolOp():   # always evaluates every part (no short-circuit) → random draws stay identical
            parts = [evaluate(v, ctx) for v in node.values]
            return np.logical_and.reduce(parts) if isinstance(node.op, ast.And) else np.logical_or.reduce(parts)
        case ast.Compare():  ...   # chained comparisons, combined with logical_and
        case ast.IfExp():    return np.where(evaluate(node.test, ctx), evaluate(node.body, ctx), evaluate(node.orelse, ctx))
        case ast.Call():     return call_function(node, ctx)   # count, sum, mean, random...

def count(inner, ctx):     # count(FIRE) or count(nb >= 4)
    return sum(np.asarray(evaluate(inner, ctx.with_neighbour(nb)), dtype=int) for nb in ctx.neighbours)
```

**Done when:** unit tests pass on a small hand-made grid. For example, `count(FIRE) >= 1` on a 3×3 grid with one fire marks exactly its 4 neighbours, and `__import__('os')` is rejected.

## Step 4: neighbourhoods and edges (`neighbourhood.py`)

- Pad the grid once per step: `np.pad(grid, r, mode="wrap")`, or `mode="constant"` with the edge value.
- Each neighbour is then just a shifted slice of the padded array, with no loops over cells:

```python
def neighbour_views(grid, offsets, edges):
    r = max(abs(c) for off in offsets for c in off)
    padded = np.pad(grid, r, mode="wrap") if edges.type == "wrap" \
             else np.pad(grid, r, mode="constant", constant_values=edges.value)
    if grid.ndim == 1:
        return [padded[r + d : r + d + grid.shape[0]] for (d,) in offsets]
    H, W = grid.shape
    return [padded[r + dr : r + dr + H, r + dc : r + dc + W] for dr, dc in offsets]
```
The offsets are: elementary `[(-1,), (1,)]`, von Neumann `[(-1,0),(1,0),(0,-1),(0,1)]`, and Moore adds the 4 diagonals.

**Done when:** a test confirms that a wrap-around grid's corner cell "sees" the opposite edges.

## Step 5: one step of the automaton (`engine.py`)

```python
def step(spec, grid, rng):
    ctx = Context(self=grid, neighbours=neighbour_views(grid, spec.offsets, spec.edges),
                  constants=spec.constants, rng=rng)
    new = np.array(np.broadcast_to(evaluate(spec.otherwise, ctx), grid.shape), dtype=grid.dtype)
    decided = np.zeros(grid.shape, dtype=bool)
    for rule in spec.rules:                      # first matching rule wins
        when = np.broadcast_to(evaluate(rule.when, ctx), grid.shape)
        then = np.broadcast_to(evaluate(rule.then, ctx), grid.shape)   # always evaluated → fixed draw order
        mask = when & ~decided
        new[mask] = then[mask]
        decided |= mask
    return new
```

**Table rules (Rule 30):** combine the neighbourhood into one index per cell, e.g. `index = left*4 + self*2 + right`. Then `lookup[index]` reads the result from an array built from the table at load time.

**Done when:** your lab example works (Rule 58: `0001100` → `0011010`), and the forest fire grid from the brief matches its known generation 1.

## Step 6: initial world and random numbers (`randomness.py`, part of `engine.py`)

- **One generator per run:** `rng = np.random.Generator(np.random.PCG64(seed))`. If the experiment has no seed, pick one and **write it into the run folder**.
- **`random()` in a rule** returns `rng.random(grid.shape)`. Because every rule is evaluated every step, in the same order, the draws are always identical.
- **Initial worlds:**
  - `text`: map characters through the legend
  - `random`: `rng.choice(states, size=shape, p=weights)`
  - `single`: one cell in the centre
  - `file`: load a saved generation
- **The generator's state** is a small dictionary (`rng.bit_generator.state`) that can be saved as JSON and restored exactly.

**Done when:** two random forest fire runs with seed 7 give identical grids at step 50, and seed 8 gives a different one.

## Step 7: the run loop and fingerprints (`fingerprints.py`, `engine.py`)

```python
def fingerprint(grid):
    h = hashlib.blake2b(digest_size=16)
    h.update(f"{grid.shape}{grid.dtype.str}".encode())
    h.update(np.ascontiguousarray(grid).tobytes())
    return h.digest()

class CycleTracker:
    def __init__(self): self.first_seen, self.order, self.cycle = {}, [], None
    def add(self, fp, t):
        if fp in self.first_seen and self.cycle is None:
            mu = self.first_seen[fp]
            self.cycle = (mu, t - mu)            # run-up length μ, cycle length λ
        self.first_seen.setdefault(fp, t); self.order.append(fp)
```

**The loop:**
1. Fingerprint step 0.
2. Then, every step: compute the new grid, fingerprint it, feed it to the questions, store the generation if enabled, and checkpoint every K steps.
3. Stop when all questions are answered, a cycle is found (the future is then known), or `max_steps` is reached.

**Done when:** Rule 30 on a ring of 8 with one live cell reports run-up 1 and cycle length 40, as we computed for Deliverable 1.

## Step 8: the five questions (`questions.py`)

Each question is a small object that "watches" the run and fills in its answer:

| Question | How it gets its answer |
|---|---|
| `state_after(n)` | saves the grid when `t == n`. If a cycle is already known and n is beyond it, re-simulates to step `μ + (n − μ) mod λ` |
| `count_after(X, n)` | the same, then counts X |
| `stable_when` | the first t where `fp(t) == fp(t − 1)`. Otherwise "cycle of length λ, never stable" or "not decided within max_steps" |
| `occurs(C)` | fingerprints C once, then compares each step. "Never" is certain once the cycle has closed without it |
| `cycle` | read from the `CycleTracker` |

**For random rules:** answers say "grid repeated, but the rules are random, so this is not a guaranteed cycle".

**Done when:** the forest fire experiment prints all five answers and they match the known ones (stable from step 5, 2 trees after 3 steps, …).

## Step 9: saving, reloading and resuming (`storage.py`)

- **A folder per run** containing copies of `automaton.json` and `experiment.json` (with the real seed), then `checkpoint.npz`, `generations.npz`, `answers.json`.
- **The checkpoint** holds the whole `RunState`: grid, step, `json.dumps(rng.bit_generator.state)`, the fingerprint list (as an array of shape `(T, 16)`), the answers so far, and a digest of the spec file.
- **Atomic writes:** write to `checkpoint.tmp`, then `os.replace(...)`, so a crash never leaves a half-written file.
- **Ctrl+C:** catch `KeyboardInterrupt` in the loop, save a checkpoint, and print "Stopped at step 412. Continue with: cellab resume runs/…".
- **`resume`:**
  1. load the checkpoint
  2. refuse if the spec digest changed
  3. restore the generator state and the fingerprint table
  4. continue the same loop from `step + 1`

**Done when:** the most important test passes: **100 steps in one go equals 40 steps, stop, resume, 60 steps**, with identical fingerprints and answers. Test it on a random automaton, so the generator state is checked too.

## Step 10: the command line (`cli.py`)

Four `argparse` subcommands that only call the layers above:
- `cellab check automata/forest_fire.json`: validate only.
- `cellab run experiments/forest_fire_brief.json [--steps N] [--seed S]`: run, answer, save.
- `cellab resume runs/.../<run> [--steps K]`.
- `cellab render runs/.../<run> --gif`.

**Done when:** you can run the whole demo from the terminal.

## Step 11: pictures (`render.py`)

- **Images:** map each state to a colour (an optional `colors` field in the spec, used for display only), scale up with nearest-neighbour, and save as PNG.
- **Animation:** 2D runs become an animated GIF via Pillow.
- **1D runs:** stack the rows over time into one image (the classic Rule 30 triangle).

**Done when:** the brief's forest fire burns in a GIF. This material goes straight into the slides.

## Step 12: tests (`tests/`, written alongside each step)

- **Known results:**
  - Rule 58 (lab example)
  - Rule 30 cycle lengths
  - Rule 90: any start on a 16-cell ring dies within 8 steps
  - forest fire answers
  - the brief's sandpile settles at `1 3 2 / 0 2 3 / 3 0 1`
- **Same seed twice is identical; different seeds differ.**
- **Resume equals uninterrupted** (step 9).
- **Broken files:** `tests/invalid/*.json`, each with its expected error.
- **Generality guard:** no state name from `automata/*.json` appears anywhere in `cellab/*.py`.

## Step 13: more automata, files only (day 6)

Add sandpile, cyclic, voter, crystal growth, epidemic, diffusion, traffic (Rule 184) and Game of Life, each with an experiment and a test where a known result exists. Any automaton that needs a code change exposes a gap in the rule language. Fix the language, never add an `if automaton == ...`.

## Assistant (2026-10-29T22:08:17.479Z)

Yes, you've got it. This week is only the engine. No machine learning, and no natural language parsing yet.

## What we're building this week

A program that **reads a description of an automaton from a file and runs it**. The file isn't Python code. It's a short text file in our own simple format: our "made-up program", as you put it.

Think of a **music player**. It doesn't contain any songs. You give it a song file and it plays it, and a new song needs no change to the player. Our engine is the player, and each automaton is a song file.

## In practice

You write a file like this, `forest_fire.json`:

```json
{
  "states": ["EMPTY", "TREE", "FIRE"],
  "neighbourhood": "von_neumann",
  "rules": [
    {"when": "self == FIRE", "then": "EMPTY"},
    {"when": "self == TREE and count(FIRE) >= 1", "then": "FIRE"}
  ]
}
```

and a second small file saying which grid to start from, how many steps to run, and which questions to answer. Then you type:

```bash
cellab run experiments/forest_fire.json
```

and the engine:
1. **Reads the files** and checks they make sense. A typo like `FLAME` gets a clear error.
2. **Runs the automaton** step by step.
3. **Answers the 5 questions**: state after N, when it's stable, whether a configuration occurs, how many trees, whether it cycles.
4. **Saves everything** to a folder.

For Brian's Brain you write a different file and run the same command. The engine code never changes; the professor's note "nothing specific to one automaton in the code" means exactly this.

## The three extra things the professor asked for

1. **Save and resume.** If you stop a run halfway (or it crashes), you can load it and it continues from where it stopped, as if nothing happened.
2. **Fingerprints (hashes).** After every step the engine computes a short code that identifies the grid. If the same code appears twice, the automaton has repeated a state. That's how it answers "is it stable?" and "does it cycle?" without comparing whole grids.
3. **Fixed randomness.** Some automata use chance, like lightning starting fires. With a fixed seed, running twice gives exactly the same result, so any run can be reproduced.

## How this fits the whole project

| Deliverable | What gets added |
|---|---|
| **2 (this week)** | The engine: files in, simulation + answers out |
| 3 | Machine learning: the engine generates thousands of runs as training data |
| 4 | Language parsing: AI turns an English description into the file format above |
| Final | An interface on top of everything |

So this week, no AI, just solid ordinary code. Everything later depends on it: the machine learning trains on runs the engine produces, and the parser in Deliverable 4 has to produce files in exactly this format.

## Assistant (2026-10-29T22:10:00.215Z)

Yes, I'm sure. Here's the official line for Deliverable 2, word for word:

> **L6 — Deliverable 2:** "Modeling an automata within your system: world state and rules, experiment parameters, state storage and recovery."

Your Lab 5 notes match it: rules from files, save and resume, parameters, hashes, fixed seeds. Neither mentions machine learning or language models. Those come in Deliverable 3 (Lab 11, after the neural networks lab) and Deliverable 4 (Lab 13, after the Bayesian networks lab).

## Why it's still AI

The course seems to follow the classic order of an AI subject. Judging from the lab exercises:

| Labs | Topic | Kind of AI |
|---|---|---|
| L2 | modelling and solving a decision problem | classical AI: state spaces and search |
| L5 | constraint satisfaction | classical AI: constraints |
| L9 | neural networks | machine learning |
| L12 | Bayesian networks | probabilistic reasoning |

Deliverable 2 sits in the classical-AI half. "Modelling" in an AI course has a specific meaning: describing a problem as a **state space**. You define the states, an initial state, the transitions between states, and a goal test. That's exactly what the engine does:

| AI concept (from the labs) | In our Deliverable 2 |
|---|---|
| State | the grid at one moment |
| Initial state | the starting world from the experiment file |
| Transition function | one step of the rules |
| Goal test | "does configuration C occur?", "is it stable?" |
| Visited set in a search (avoids going in circles) | the fingerprint table of hashes |
| Reachability | "is C ever reached from this start?" |
| Constraint checking (Lab 5) | validating the input file |

The professor's "hashes over states" point is the visited set from search algorithms, applied to automata. So when presenting, use these AI terms. The work stays the same, but the professor will see the course material in it.

## An optional extra that adds visible AI

To put actual AI problem-solving into this deliverable, there's a natural extra that uses the Lab 5 topic directly. The engine answers the forward question: "starting here, where do we end up?" The reverse question, **"which starting grid leads to this grid?"**, is a constraint satisfaction problem:
- Each cell of the unknown previous grid is a variable with values 0 or 1.
- Each cell of the known grid gives a constraint, e.g. "left, me and right must produce 1 under Rule 30".
- A backtracking solver either finds a previous grid or proves none exists.

Grids with no possible previous grid have a name: **"Garden of Eden" configurations**. Finding them is a well-known topic, and it's a nice small research result for the presentation.

It fits the long-term goals from your notes too: beyond what's asked, a research angle, and directly tied to the lab. It's a stretch goal, though. The engine and the checklist come first.

So: no machine learning this week is correct and expected. But the deliverable is still AI, and we can make that visible.

{
  "file_path": "D:\\CelLab\\src\\cellab\\neighbourhood.py",
  "content": "\"\"\"Which cells a cell can see, and what lies beyond the edges of the grid.\n\nA neighbourhood is a list of offsets relative to a cell: (-1, 0) is the cell above,\n(0, 1) the cell to the right, (-1,) the cell to the left in a 1D row.\n\nTo hand every cell its neighbours at once, the grid is padded with `radius` extra\ncells on every side: copied from the opposite side for \"wrap\" edges, or filled with\na fixed value for \"fixed\" edges. Each neighbour is then a shifted view (a slice) of\nthe padded grid, so no loop over cells is ever needed.\n\n    padded grid (radius 1, wrap)        the view for offset (-1, 0) (\"north\")\n    . . . . . . .                       is the padded grid shifted down by one:\n    . a b c d e .                       every cell sees the cell above it.\n    . f g h i j .\n    . . . . . . .\n\"\"\"\n\nimport numpy as np\n\n# name -> (dimensions, offsets in reading order)\nNAMED_NEIGHBOURHOODS: dict[str, tuple[int, tuple[tuple[int, ...], ...]]] = {\n    \"elementary\": (1, ((-1,), (1,))),\n    \"von_neumann\": (2, ((-1, 0), (0, -1), (0, 1), (1, 0))),\n    \"moore\": (2, tuple((dr, dc) for dr in (-1, 0, 1) for dc in (-1, 0, 1) if (dr, dc) != (0, 0))),\n}\n\n# Single neighbours that rules can name directly, whatever the neighbourhood is.\nDIRECTIONS: dict[int, dict[str, tuple[int, ...]]] = {\n    1: {\"left\": (-1,), \"right\": (1,)},\n    2: {\n        \"north\": (-1, 0), \"south\": (1, 0), \"west\": (0, -1), \"east\": (0, 1),\n        \"north_west\": (-1, -1), \"north_east\": (-1, 1), \"south_west\": (1, -1), \"south_east\": (1, 1),\n    },\n}\n\n\ndef resolve_neighbourhood(raw, dimensions: int) -> tuple[tuple[int, ...], ...]:\n    \"\"\"Turn the `neighbourhood` field of a file into a tuple of offsets.\n\n    Accepts a name (\"elementary\", \"von_neumann\", \"moore\") or an explicit list of\n    offsets such as [[-1, 0], [1, 0]]. Raises ValueError with a readable message.\n    \"\"\"\n    if isinstance(raw, str):\n        if raw not in NAMED_NEIGHBOURHOODS:\n            raise ValueError(f\"unknown neighbourhood '{raw}' (known: {', '.join(NAMED_NEIGHBOURHOODS)}, \"\n                             \"or a list of offsets)\")\n        dims, offsets = NAMED_NEIGHBOURHOODS[raw]\n        if dims != dimensions:\n            raise ValueError(f\"'{raw}' is a {dims}D neighbourhood, but the automaton has {dimensions} dimension(s)\")\n        return offsets\n\n    if isinstance(raw, list) and raw:\n        offsets: list[tuple[int, ...]] = []\n        for item in raw:\n            if (not isinstance(item, list) or len(item) != dimensions\n                    or not all(isinstance(v, int) and not isinstance(v, bool) for v in item)):\n                raise ValueError(f\"offset {item!r} must be a list of {dimensions} whole number(s)\")\n            offset = tuple(item)\n            if not any(offset):\n                raise ValueError(\"the cell itself (offset of zeros) is not a neighbour; use 'self' in rules\")\n            if offset in offsets:\n                raise ValueError(f\"offset {item!r} is listed twice\")\n            offsets.append(offset)\n        return tuple(offsets)\n\n    raise ValueError(\"must be a neighbourhood name or a non-empty list of offsets\")\n\n\ndef pattern_offsets(offsets: tuple[tuple[int, ...], ...]) -> tuple[tuple[int, ...], ...]:\n    \"\"\"The cells a table rule reads: the neighbours plus the cell itself, in reading order.\n\n    For the elementary neighbourhood this is (left, self, right).\n    \"\"\"\n    zero = tuple(0 for _ in offsets[0])\n    return tuple(sorted(set(offsets) | {zero}))\n\n\nclass GridViews:\n    \"\"\"A padded copy of a grid that hands out the grid shifted by any offset.\"\"\"\n\n    def __init__(self, grid: np.ndarray, radius: int, edge_mode: str, edge_value):\n        self.shape = grid.shape\n        self.radius = radius\n        if edge_mode == \"wrap\":\n            self.padded = np.pad(grid, radius, mode=\"wrap\")\n        else:\n            self.padded = np.pad(grid, radius, mode=\"constant\", constant_values=edge_value)\n\n    def at(self, offset: tuple[int, ...]) -> np.ndarray:\n        \"\"\"The value of the neighbour at `offset`, for every cell at once.\"\"\"\n        slices = tuple(slice(self.radius + d, self.radius + d + n) for d, n in zip(offset, self.shape))\n        return self.padded[slices]\n"
}

ast.Constant):\n        return node.value\n    if isinstance(node, ast.Name):\n        return nb if node.id == \"nb\" else ctx.value_of(node.id)\n    if isinstance(node, ast.BinOp):\n        return            return np.invert(value)\n        return value\n    if isinstance(node, ast.BoolOp):\n        parts = [_evaluate(part, ctx, nb) for part in node.values]   # all parts, always\n        combine = np.logical_and if isinstance(node.op, ast.And) else np.logical_or\n        return functools.reduce(combine, parts)\n    if isinstance(node, ast.Compare):\n        left, result = in AGGREGATES and len(args) == 1:\n        return _aggregate(name, args[0], ctx)\n    if name == \"random\":\n        return ctx.rng.random(ctx.shape)\n    values = [_evaluate(arg, ctx, nb) for arg in args]\n    if name == \"min\":\n        return functools.reduce(np.minimum, values)\n    if name == \"max\":\n        return functools.reduce(np.maximum, values)\n    if name == \"abs\":\n round\n\n\ndef _aggregate(name: str, arg: ast.expr, ctx: EvalContext):\n    \"\"\"count/sum/mean/min/max of `arg` evaluated once per neighbour.\"\"\"\n    if name == \"count\" and isinstance(arg, ast.Name) and arg.id in ctx.state_values:\n        target = ctx.state_values[arg.id]                       # count(NAME) shorthand\n        per_neighbour = [neighbour == target for neighbour in stacked.sum(axis=0)\n    if name == \"mean\":\n        return stacked.mean(axis=0)\n    if name == \"min\":\n        return stacked.min(axis=0)\n    return stacked.max(axis=0)\n"

{

  "content": "\"\"\"Grids written as text, used in experiment files and in printed answers.\n\nA grid is a list of rows. A row is read in one of two ways:\n\n    \"TT.F\"          no spaces: every character is one cell\n    \"0 12 3\"        with spaces: every word is one cell (for long names or numbers)\n\nEach cell is looked up in the legend first (e.g. {\"T\": \"TREE\"}) and otherwise read\ndirectly as a state (a state name or a number). A 1D grid is exactly one row.\n\"\"\"\n\nimport numpy as np\n\nfrom .states import StateSpace\n\n\ndef split_row(text: str) -> list[str]:\n    \"\"\"'TT.F' -> ['T', 'T', '.', 'F'];  '0 12 3' -> ['0', '12', '3']\"\"\"\n    text = text.strip()\n    return text.split() if any(ch.isspace() for ch in text) else list(text)\n\n\ndef parse_legend(raw: dict, states: StateSpace) -> dict[str, int | float]:\n    \"\"\"{\"T\": \"TREE\"} -> {\"T\": 1}. Raises ValueError with a readable message.\"\"\"\n    legend = {}\n    for token, value in raw.items():\n        if not token or any(ch.isspace() for ch in token):\n            raise ValueError(f\"legend key {token!r} must be text without spaces\")\n        try:\n            legend[token] = states.parse(value)\n        except ValueError as error:\n            raise ValueError(f\"legend '{token}': {error}\") from None\n    return legend\n\n\ndef parse_grid(rows: list[str], states: StateSpace, dimensions: int,\n               legend: dict[str, int | float] | None = None) -> np.ndarray:\n    \"\"\"Read a grid written as text rows. Raises ValueError with a readable message.\"\"\"\n    legend = legend or {}\n    if dimensions == 1 and len(rows) != 1:\n        raise ValueError(f\"a 1D grid is written as exactly one row (got {len(rows)})\")\n    table = []\n    for number, row in enumerate(rows, start=1):\n        tokens = split_row(row)\n        if not tokens:\n            raise ValueError(f\"row {number} is empty\")\n        values = []\n        for token in tokens:\n            if token in legend:\n                values.append(legend[token])\n                continue\n            try:\n                values.append(states.parse(token))\n            except ValueError as error:\n                raise ValueError(f\"row {number}, '{token}': not in the legend, and {error}\") from None\n        table.append(values)\n    if len({len(values) for values in table}) > 1:\n        raise ValueError(\"all rows must have the same number of cells\")\n    grid = np.array(table, dtype=states.dtype)\n    return grid[0] if dimensions == 1 else grid\n\n\ndef format_grid(grid: np.ndarray, states: StateSpace, legend: dict[str, int | float] | None = None) -> list[str]:\n    \"\"\"Write a grid as text rows, using the legend's symbols where possible.\"\"\"\n    symbol_for = {}\n    for token, value in (legend or {}).items():\n        symbol_for.setdefault(value, token)\n    rows = grid[np.newaxis] if grid.ndim == 1 else grid\n    tokens = [[symbol_for.get(value.item(), None) or states.format(value) for value in row] for row in rows]\n    joiner = \"\" if all(len(token) == 1 for row in tokens for token in row) else \" \"\n    return [joiner.join(row) for row in tokens]\n"
}

Both answer the same question for every cell at once:\n\n    \"does this rule apply here, and if so, what is the new value?\"\n\nand return it as two arrays the size of the grid: `applies` (True/False) and\n`values`. The engine (engine.py) combines the rules: the first rule that applies\nto a cell decides its new value.\n\nExpressionRule   {\"when\": \"<condition>\", \"then\": \"<new value>\"}\nTableRule        {\"table\": {\"111\": 0, \"110\": 0, ...}}\n                 The table lists patterns of (neighbours + the cell itself, in\n                 reading order) and the value each pattern produces. Patterns not\n                 listed fall through to the next rule.\n\"\"\"\n\nfrom dataclasses import dataclass\n\nimport numpy as np\n\nfrom .errors import InputFileError\nfrom .expressions import EvalContext, Expression\nfrom .grids import split_row\nfrom .neighbourhood import pattern_offsets\nfrom .states import StateSpace\n\nMAX_TABLE_SIZE = 1_000_000   # number of possible patterns a table may cover\n\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True, eq=False)\nclass ExpressionRule:\n    where: str\n    when: Expression\n    then: Expression\n\n    @property\n    def uses_random(self) -> bool:\n        return self.when.uses_random or self.then.uses_random\n\n    def evaluate(self, ctx: EvalContext) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:\n        # Both parts are always evaluated, so random() draws happen in a fixed order.\n        applies = np.broadcast_to(np.asarray(self.when.evaluate(ctx), dtype=bool), ctx.shape)\n        values = np.broadcast_to(self.then.evaluate(ctx), ctx.shape)\n        return applies, values\n\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True, eq=False)\nclass TableRule:\n    where: str\n    offsets: tuple[tuple[int, ...], ...]   # cells read, in pattern order\n    base: int                              # number of possible values per cell\n    lowest: int                            # the smallest possible value\n    listed: np.ndarray                     # listed[code]  -> is this pattern in the table?\n    results: np.ndarray                    # results[code] -> the value it produces\n\n    uses_random = False\n\n    def evaluate(self, ctx: EvalContext) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:\n        # Each pattern becomes a number (\"code\"), like reading the cells as digits in base `base`.\n        code = np.zeros(ctx.shape, dtype=np.int64)\n        for offset in self.offsets:\n            cell = ctx.grid if not any(offset) else ctx.views.at(offset)\n            code = code * self.base + (cell.astype(np.int64) - self.lowest)\n        return self.listed[code], self.results[code]\n\n\ndef build_table_rule(table: dict, where: str, file: str, states: StateSpace,\n                     neighbour_offsets: tuple[tuple[int, ...], ...]) -> TableRule:\n    \"\"\"Check a table from a file and turn it into lookup arrays.\"\"\"\n    def fail(message: str):\n        raise InputFileError(file, where, message)\n\n    if states.kind == \"real\":\n        fail(\"tables need named states or integer states with a min and a max\")\n    if states.kind == \"integer\" and (states.minimum is None or states.maximum is None):\n        fail(\"tables on integer states need both 'min' and 'max' in \\\"states\\\"\")\n    if not table:\n        fail(\"the table is empty\")\n\n    offsets = pattern_offsets(neighbour_offsets)\n    lowest = int(states.lowest)\n    base = int(states.highest) - lowest + 1\n    size = base ** len(offsets)\n    if size > MAX_TABLE_SIZE:\n        fail(f\"the table would cover {size:,} possible patterns; use when/then rules instead\")\n\n    listed = np.zeros(size, dtype=bool)\n    results = np.zeros(size, dtype=np.int64)\n    for pattern, result in table.items():\n        tokens = split_row(pattern)\n        if len(tokens) != len(offsets):\n            fail(f\"pattern '{pattern}' has {len(tokens)} cells, but each pattern lists \"\n                 f\"{len(offsets)} (the neighbours and the cell itself, in reading order)\")\n        code = 0\n        for token in tokens:\n            try:\n                value = int(states.parse(token))\n            except ValueError as error:\n                fail(f\"pattern '{pattern}': {error}\")\n            code = code * base + (value - lowest)\n        if listed[code]:\n            fail(f\"pattern '{pattern}' is listed twice\")\n        try:\n            results[code] = int(states.parse(result))\n        except ValueError as error:\n            fail(f\"pattern '{pattern}' -> {result!r}: {error}\")\n        listed[code] = True\n    return TableRule(where=where, offsets=offsets, base=base, lowest=lowest, listed=listed, results=results)\n"

{

  "content": "\"\"\"One step of an automaton: old grid in, new grid out.\n\nThis is the whole simulation. Everything is computed from the OLD grid, for all\ncells at the same time, so the order of cells never matters.\n\n    1. Widen the grid to a roomy number type (no overflow surprises in rules).\n    2. Pad it and prepare the neighbour views                    (neighbourhood.py)\n    3. Start every cell from the `otherwise` value (usually: unchanged).\n    4. Go through the rules in file order. A rule only changes cells that no\n       earlier rule has claimed: the first rule that applies to a cell wins.\n    5. Check the new values (whole numbers, inside the declared states) and\n       store them in the grid's normal type.                      (states.py)\n\nThe function never touches files, and its only side effect is drawing random\nnumbers from the generator it is given. That is what makes runs reproducible.\n\"\"\"\n\nimport numpy as np\n\nfrom .automaton import Automaton\nfrom .errors import RuleError\nfrom .expressions import EvalContext\nfrom .neighbourhood import GridViews\n\n\ndef step(automaton: Automaton, grid: np.ndarray, rng: np.random.Generator, step_number: int) -> np.ndarray:\n    \"\"\"Compute the generation after `grid`. `step_number` is the number of `grid` itself.\"\"\"\n    states = automaton.states\n    values = grid.astype(states.work_dtype)\n    views = GridViews(values, automaton.radius, automaton.edge_mode, automaton.edge_value)\n    ctx = EvalContext(values, views, automaton.neighbour_offsets, automaton.dimensions,\n                      automaton.constants, states.constants(), rng, step_number)\n\n    work = np.empty(grid.shape, dtype=states.work_dtype)\n    work[...] = _cell_values(np.broadcast_to(automaton.otherwise.evaluate(ctx), grid.shape),\n                             states.kind, automaton.otherwise.where)\n\n    decided = np.zeros(grid.shape, dtype=bool)\n    for rule in automaton.rules:\n        applies, new_values = rule.evaluate(ctx)\n        chosen = applies & ~decided            # cells this rule decides\n        if chosen.any():\n            work[chosen] = _cell_values(new_values[chosen], states.kind, rule.where)\n            decided |= chosen\n\n    try:\n        return states.finish_step(work)\n    except RuleError as error:\n        raise RuleError(f\"step {step_number} -> {step_number + 1}: {error}\") from None\n\n\ndef _cell_values(values: np.ndarray, kind: str, where: str) -> np.ndarray:\n    \"\"\"Check values a rule produced before they are stored in a grid.\"\"\"\n    values = np.asarray(values)\n    if kind == \"real\":\n        if np.isnan(values).any():\n            raise RuleError(f\"{where}: produced a value that is not a number (NaN)\")\n        return values\n    if values.dtype.kind == \"f\":\n        if not np.all(np.isfinite(values)) or not np.all(values == np.floor(values)):\n            bad = values[~(np.isfinite(values) & (values == np.floor(values)))][0]\n            raise RuleError(f\"{where}: produced {bad:g}, which is not a whole number \"\n                            \"(use // instead of /, or round())\")\n        return values.astype(np.int64)\n    return values\n"
}

  "content": "\"\"\"Seeded random numbers: the same seed always gives the same run.\n\nA run owns exactly one generator, created from its seed. Nothing in CelLab uses\nPython's `random` module or NumPy's global random functions (a test checks this),\nso the only randomness in a run comes from this generator, drawn in a fixed order:\n\n    1. the random initial world (if the experiment asks for one)\n    2. then, every step, one full-grid array per random() in the rules, in file order\n\nThe generator's internal state is a small dictionary. It is saved in every\ncheckpoint, so a resumed run continues the exact same random sequence.\n\"\"\"\n\nimport json\nimport secrets\n\nimport numpy as np\n\n\ndef new_seed() -> int:\n    \"\"\"A fresh seed for runs whose experiment file does not give one (it is recorded).\"\"\"\n    return secrets.randbelow(2**32)\n\n\ndef make_generator(seed: int) -> np.random.Generator:\n    return np.random.Generator(np.random.PCG64(seed))\n\n\ndef generator_state(rng: np.random.Generator) -> str:\n    \"\"\"The generator's full internal state, as JSON text.\"\"\"\n    return json.dumps(rng.bit_generator.state)\n\n\ndef restore_generator(state: str) -> np.random.Generator:\n    \"\"\"A generator that continues exactly where the saved one stopped.\"\"\"\n    rng = np.random.Generator(np.random.PCG64())\n    rng.bit_generator.state = json.loads(state)\n    return rng\n"
}

{
  "file_path": "D:\\CelLab\\src\\cellab\\fingerprints.py",
  "content": "\"\"\"Fingerprints (hashes) of grids, and the history of a run built from them.\n\nA fingerprint is a 16-byte BLAKE2b hash of a grid's contents, shape and number\ntype. Two different grids get the same fingerprint with a probability of about\n1 in 2^128, so in practice equal fingerprints mean equal grids, and comparing 16\nbytes is much cheaper than comparing whole grids.\n\nThe History remembers the fingerprint of every step and the first step at which\neach fingerprint appeared. That is enough to answer three of the five questions:\n\n    the first repeat      fingerprint(t) was already seen at step s  ->  cycle from s, length t - s\n    the first standstill  fingerprint(t) == fingerprint(t - 1)       ->  stable from t - 1\n    \"does C occur?\"       look C's fingerprint up in `first_seen`\n\"\"\"\n\nimport hashlib\n\nimport numpy as np\n\nFINGERPRINT_SIZE = 16   # bytes\n\n\ndef fingerprint(grid: np.ndarray) -> bytes:\n    h = hashlib.blake2b(digest_size=FINGERPRINT_SIZE)\n    h.update(f\"{grid.shape}|{grid.dtype.str}|\".encode())\n    h.update(np.ascontiguousarray(grid).tobytes())\n    return h.digest()\n\n\nclass History:\n    \"\"\"Fingerprints of every step of a run, step 0 included.\"\"\"\n\n    def __init__(self):\n        self.fingerprints: list[bytes] = []          # index = step number\n        self.first_seen: dict[bytes, int] = {}       # fingerprint -> first step with it\n        self.repeat: tuple[int, int] | None = None   # (earlier step, later step) of the first repeat\n        self.standstill: int | None = None           # first step t with grid(t) == grid(t - 1)\n\n    @property\n    def last_step(self) -> int:\n        return len(self.fingerprints) - 1\n\n    @property\n    def cycle(self) -> tuple[int, int] | None:\n        \"\"\"(first step of the cycle, cycle length), once a grid has repeated.\"\"\"\n        if self.repeat is None:\n            return None\n        earlier, later = self.repeat\n        return earlier, later - earlier\n\n    def record(self, fp: bytes) -> None:\n        \"\"\"Add the fingerprint of the next step.\"\"\"\n        step = len(self.fingerprints)\n        if fp in self.first_seen:\n            if self.repeat is None:\n                self.repeat = (self.first_seen[fp], step)\n        else:\n            self.first_seen[fp] = step\n        if self.standstill is None and self.fingerprints and fp == self.fingerprints[-1]:\n            self.standstill = step\n        self.fingerprints.append(fp)\n\n    @classmethod\n    def rebuild(cls, fingerprints: list[bytes]) -> \"History\":\n        \"\"\"Recreate a History from a saved list of fingerprints (used when resuming).\"\"\"\n        history = cls()\n        for fp in fingerprints:\n            history.record(fp)\n        return history\n"
}

Values without a\ncolour get one from a default palette (named states) or a light-to-dark shade\n(numbers, scaled between the smallest and largest value in the run).\n\"\"\"\n\nfrom pathlib import Path\n\nimport numpy as np\nfrom PIL import Image\n\nfrom .automaton import Automaton\nfrom .experiment import load_experiment\nfrom .storage import RunFolder\n\nDEFAULT_PALETTE = [(245, 243, 238), (22, 32, 43), (216, 90, 48), (74, 115, 38), (43, 92, 153),\n                   (239, 159, 39), (153, 53, 86), (29, 158, 117), (136, 135, 128), (127, 119, 221)]\nLIGHT, DARK = np.array([245, 243, 238], float), np.array([22, 32, 43], float)\nMAX_GIF_FRAMES = 300\n\n\ndef painter(automaton: Automaton, values: np.ndarray):\n    \"\"\"A function that turns a grid (or a stack of grids) into RGB colours.\"\"\"\n    states = automaton.states\n    if states.kind == \"named\":\n        table = np.array([automaton.colors.get(i, DEFAULT_PALETTE[i % len(DEFAULT_PALETTE)])\n                          for i in range(len(states.names))], dtype=np.uint8)\n        return lambda grid: table[grid]\n\n    low = float(values.min()) if states.minimum is None else float(states.minimum)\n    high = float(values.max()) if states.maximum is None else float(states.maximum)\n    span = (high - low) or 1.0\n\n    def paint(grid):\n        share = np.clip((grid.astype(float) - low) / span, 0, 1)[..., np.newaxis]\n        rgb = (LIGHT + share * (DARK - LIGHT)).astype(np.uint8)\n        for value, colour in automaton.colors.items():\n            rgb[grid == value] = colour\n        return rgb\n\n    return paint\n\n\ndef to_image(rgb: np.ndarray, cell: int) -> Image.Image:\n    if rgb.ndim == 2:                       # a single 1D row\n        rgb = rgb[np.newaxis]\n    height, width = rgb.shape[:2]\n    return Image.fromarray(rgb, \"RGB\").resize((width * cell, height * cell), Image.NEAREST)\n\n\ndef cell_size(height: int, width: int, target: int = 480) -> int:\n    return max(1, min(24, target // max(height, width)))\n\n\ndef render_run(path: str | Path, out_dir: str | Path | None = None, frame_ms: int = 120) -> list[Path]:\n    \"\"\"Make pictures of a run folder's stored generations. Returns the files written.\"\"\"\n    folder = RunFolder(path)\n    experiment = load_experiment(folder.file(RunFolder.EXPERIMENT))\n    automaton = experiment.automaton\n    generations = folder.read_all_generations(experiment.shape, automaton.states.dtype)\n    out = Path(out_dir) if out_dir else folder.path\n    out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)\n    paint = painter(automaton, generations)\n    written = []\n\n    if automaton.dimensions == 1:\n        rgb = paint(generations)                                   # (time, cells, 3)\n        image = to_image(rgb, cell_size(*rgb.shape[:2], target=720))\n        image.save(out / \"spacetime.png\")\n        return [out / \"spacetime.png\"]\n\n    cell = cell_size(*experiment.shape)\n    for name, grid in ((\"first.png\", generations[0]), (\"last.png\", generations[-1])):\n        to_image(paint(grid), cell).save(out / name)\n        written.append(out / name)\n\n    chosen = generations\n    if len(generations) > MAX_GIF_FRAMES:\n        chosen = generations[np.linspace(0, len(generations) - 1, MAX_GIF_FRAMES).astype(int)]\n    frames = [to_image(paint(grid), cell) for grid in chosen]\n    frames[0].save(out / \"run.gif\", save_all=True, append_images=frames[1:], duration=frame_ms, loop=0)\n    written.append(out / \"run.gif\")\n    return written\n"

The\ntests run the engine and these side by side on random grids; if they ever\ndisagree, one of them is wrong.\n\"\"\"\n\nVON_NEUMANN = [(-1, 0), (0, -1), (0, 1), (1, 0)]\nMOORE = [(dr, dc) for dr in (-1, 0, 1) for dc in (-1, 0, 1) if (dr, dc) != (0, 0)]\n\n\ndef neighbours(grid, r, c, offsets, wrap, edge=None):\n    rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])\n    values = []\n    for dr, dc in offsets:\n        rr, cc = r + dr, c + dc\n        if wrap:\n            values.append(grid[rr % rows][cc % cols])\n        elif 0 <= rr < rows and 0 <= cc < cols:\n            values.append(grid[rr][cc])\n        else:\n            values.append(edge)\n    return values\n\n\ndef each_cell(grid, new_value):\n    return [[new_value(r, c) for c in range(len(grid[0]))] for r in range(len(grid))]\n\n\ndef elementary(row, rule, wrap=True, edge=0):\n    n, out = len(row), []\n    for i in range(n):\n        left = row[i - 1] if i > 0 else (row[-1] if wrap else edge)\n        right = row[i + 1] if i < n - 1 else (row[0] if wrap else edge)\n        out.append((rule >> (4 * left + 2 * row[i] + right)) & 1)\n    return out\n\n\ndef traffic(row):                      # 0 = EMPTY, 1 = CAR, circular road, cars move right\n    n = len(row)\n    return [1 if (row[i] == 1 and row[(i + 1) % n] == 1) or (row[i] == 0 and row[i - 1] == 1) else 0\n            for i in range(n)]\n\n\ndef forest_fire(grid):                 # 0 EMPTY, 1 TREE, 2 FIRE; edges are EMPTY\n    def new(r, c):\n        me = grid[r][c]\n        if me == 2:\n            return 0\n        if me == 1 and 2 in neighbours(grid, r, c, VON_NEUMANN, wrap=False, edge=0):\n            return 2\n        return me\n    return each_cell(grid, new)\n\n\ndef brians_brain(grid):                # 0 OFF, 1 FIRING, 2 DYING; wrap-around\n    def new(r, c):\n        me = grid[r][c]\n        if me == 1:\n            return 2\n        if me == 2:\n            return 0\n        return 1 if neighbours(grid, r, c, MOORE, wrap=True).count(1) == 2 else 0\n    return each_cell(grid, new)\n\n\ndef game_of_life(grid):                # 0 DEAD, 1 ALIVE; wrap-around\n    def new(r, c):\n        alive = neighbours(grid, r, c, MOORE, wrap=True).count(1)\n        return 1 if alive == 3 or (grid[r][c] == 1 and alive == 2) else 0\n    return each_cell(grid, new)\n\n\ndef sandpile(grid):                    # grains; edges hold 0 and swallow grains\n    def new(r, c):\n        me = grid[r][c]\n        gained = sum(1 for v in neighbours(grid, r, c, VON_NEUMANN, wrap=False, edge=0) if v >= 4)\n        return me - (4 if me >= 4 else 0) + gained\n    return each_cell(grid, new)\n\n\ndef cyclic(grid, levels=4, threshold=2):\n    def new(r, c):\n        nxt = (grid[r][c] + 1) % levels\n        return nxt if neighbours(grid, r, c, MOORE, wrap=True).count(nxt) >= threshold else grid[r][c]\n    return each_cell(grid, new)\n\n\ndef voter(grid):                       # 0 A, 1 B; wrap-around; ties keep the old opinion\n    def new(r, c):\n        around = neighbours(grid, r, c, MOORE, wrap=True)\n        a, b = around.count(0), around.count(1)\n        return 0 if a > b else 1 if b > a else grid[r][c]\n    return each_cell(grid, new)\n\n\ndef crystal_growth(grid, needed=1):    # 0 EMPTY, 1 CRYSTAL; edges EMPTY\n    def new(r, c):\n        if grid[r][c] == 0 and neighbours(grid, r, c, VON_NEUMANN, wrap=False, edge=0).count(1) == needed:\n            return 1\n        return grid[r][c]\n    return each_cell(grid, new)\n\n\ndef epidemic(grid):                    # 0 S, 1-3 infected for 1/2/3 turns, 4 R; edges S\n    def new(r, c):\n        me = grid[r][c]\n        if me == 0:\n            infected = sum(1 for v in neighbours(grid, r, c, MOORE, wrap=False, edge=0) if v in (1, 2, 3))\n            return 1 if infected >= 2 else 0\n        return me + 1 if me in (1, 2, 3) else me\n    return each_cell(grid, new)\n\n\ndef diffusion(grid):                   # average of self and 4 neighbours, wrap, 2 decimals\n    def new(r, c):\n        return round((grid[r][c] + sum(neighbours(grid, r, c, VON_NEUMANN, wrap=True))) / 5, 2)\n    return each_cell(grid, new)\n"

"""Plain helpers shared by the tests (fixtures live in conftest.py)."""

import json
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np

from cellab import load_automaton, load_experiment, step
from cellab.randomness import make_generator

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
AUTOMATA = ROOT / "automata"
EXPERIMENTS = ROOT / "experiments"

FOREST_FIRE = {
    "name": "Test fire",
    "dimensions": 2,
    "states": ["EMPTY", "TREE", "FIRE"],
    "neighbourhood": "von_neumann",
    "edges": {"type": "fixed", "value": "EMPTY"},
    "rules": [
        {"when": "self == FIRE", "then": "EMPTY"},
        {"when": "self == TREE and count(FIRE) >= 1", "then": "FIRE"},
    ],
}


def write_json(path: Path, data) -> Path:
    path.write_text(json.dumps(data, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
    return path


def run_steps(automaton, grid, steps, seed=0):
    """Apply the engine `steps` times; returns the list of grids including the first."""
    rng = make_generator(seed)
    grids = [np.asarray(grid, dtype=automaton.states.dtype)]
    for k in range(steps):
        grids.append(step(automaton, grids[-1], rng, k))
    return grids


def example_automaton(name: str):
    return load_automaton(AUTOMATA / f"{name}.json")


def example_experiment(name: str):
    return load_experiment(EXPERIMENTS / f"{name}.json")

signal.raise_signal(signal.SIGINT)\n\n    result = run.advance(on_step=press_ctrl_c_at_step_17)\n    assert result.stopped and run.state.step == 17\n    assert run.folder.read_status()[\"status\"] == automaton_copy.write_text(automaton_copy.read_text().replace(\"0.05\", \"0.5\"))\n    with pytest.raises(StorageError, match=\"was changed after the run started\"):\n Run.open(run.folder.path)\n    reopened.extend(15)\n    reopened.advance()\n    assert reopened.state.step == 25\n    assert reopened.state.history.fingerprints == longer.state.history.fingerprints\n\n\ndef test_opening_something_that_is_not_a_run_folder(tmp_path):\n    with pytest.raises(StorageError, match=\"not a run folder\"):\n These tests check it mechanically.\n\"\"\"\n\nimport json\nimport re\n\nimport pytest\n\nfrom cellab import Run, load_automaton, load_experiment\nfrom helpers import AUTOMATA, EXPERIMENTS, ROOT\n\n\ndef state_names() -> set[str]:\n    names = set()\n    for path in AUTOMATA.glob(\"*.json\"):\n        states = json.loads(path.read_text(encoding=\"utf-8\"))[\"states\"]\n        if isinstance(states, list):\n            names.update(name for name in states if len(name) >= 3)\n    return names\n\n\ndef test_no_state_name_from_any_example_appears_in_the_code():\n    names = state_names()\n    assert len(names) > 10                          # the check is not vacuous\n    for path in (ROOT / \"src\" / \"cellab\").glob(\"*.py\"):\n        code = path.read_text(encoding=\"utf-8\")\n        found = sorted(name for name in names if re.search(rf\"\\b{re.escape(name)}\\b\", code))\n        assert not found, f\"{path.name} mentions {found}\"\n\n\n@pytest.mark.parametrize(\"path\", sorted(AUTOMATA.glob(\"*.json\")), ids=lambda p: p.stem)\ndef test_every_example_automaton_loads(path):\n    load_automaton(path)\n\n\n@pytest.mark.parametrize(\"path\", sorted(EXPERIMENTS.glob(\"*.json\")), ids=lambda p: p.stem)\ndef test_every_example_experiment_runs_and_answers(path, tmp_path):\n    experiment = load_experiment(path)\n    run = Run.start(experiment, runs_dir=tmp_path)\n    result = run.advance()\n    assert len(result.answers) == len(experiment.questions)\n    assert run.state.step >= experiment.steps\n"
